content.title: How can Sweden prepare people for a working life shaped by AI?
content.description: Sweden’s AI ambitions are accelerating, but the workforce is not keeping pace. A growing skills gap is slowing adoption, limiting competitiveness, and risking inequality. The key question is how to equip people, organisations, and society to turn AI into real economic and social value.
content.extendedDescription: AI is already changing how work is done across Sweden. At the same time, a crucial societal question is emerging: how do we ensure that people have the skills they need to participate, contribute and thrive in a labour market where AI is becoming part of everyday working life? Sweden has strong ambitions in AI, but many employers are already reporting skills shortages and a growing gap between rapid technological development and people’s actual readiness to keep up. Demand for AI-related competence is rising quickly, while the shift is reshaping roles, learning needs and access to opportunity. This conversation explores what is required to prepare individuals, workplaces and society for the future of work — and how Sweden can make the transition both competitive and socially sustainable.

content.title: The medicines system has reached the end of the road – what can we do here and now?
content.description: Medical advances are creating new opportunities to treat diseases and improve patients' quality of life. At the same time, Sweden's medicines system faces significant challenges. The minister responsible has described the system as having reached the end of the road.
content.extendedDescription:
The government has now appointed an inquiry into medicines to review the system fundamentally. This is an important step towards a more sustainable long-term solution. But inquiries take time – and patients cannot wait.
So what can be done right now? What improvements are possible within today's system? And what concrete measures can be implemented without waiting for a larger reform?

content.title: Price tag or investment – when is a pill more than an expense?
content.description: Could a pill be society's best investment? Do we dare invest in innovation even when budgets are tight?
content.extendedDescription: The price of new medicines is often debated, but what happens if we look beyond the numbers? The seminar brings together an experienced panel with perspectives from decision-makers, government agencies, patients and healthcare for an open discussion about balancing innovation, cost-effectiveness and societal benefit. We discuss concrete challenges: how do we assess the value and societal benefits of different care interventions, and how do we prioritise when resources are limited? What risks and opportunities arise if we invest – or refrain? We are in an exciting period in which future views on medicines are being shaped, with both investments and tough cost decisions playing a role. Together, we seek new perspectives and solutions that can help people live healthier lives, transform Swedish healthcare and strengthen Sweden as a country.
content.subject: Health and social care

content.title: Litter harms animals — both wildlife and pets
content.description: Broken glass injures paws, chocolate and grape leftovers and glycol spills can poison dogs, and picnic leftovers in plastic bags or on cigarette butts can cause animals to eat the plastic too.
content.extendedDescription:
Bring your dog and join our walk against litter! We meet at 16:30 by the Söderport car park, set off towards Almedalen at 17:00 and return to our starting point at 18:00.

The walk is an initiative by Håll Sverige Rent as part of the project ‘Fan-tass-tiska perspektiv’, which approaches litter from the perspective of animals, especially pets. The walk is organised in cooperation with Gotlands kennelklubb. Members of the public, with or without dogs, are welcome to join by registering in advance: https://hallsverigerent.typeform.com/to/W5wAwUQC

The project aims to increase awareness in Sweden of the connection between litter and injuries to pets, and to influence behaviours and attitudes through this new knowledge. The project is funded by Postkodlotteriet. Svedea is also a partner and is analysing litter-related pet injuries to identify where the most important measures can be taken.

content.title: Humanoid Robotics: Is Sweden Ready for Physical AI?
content.description: Humanoid robots are leaving the labs and entering workplaces, manufacturing and everyday life. Global investments are accelerating. For Sweden – with its strong industrial base and automation heritage – the question is urgent: how do we prepare our society and industry for the new era of physical AI
content.extendedDescription:
Humanoid robots are advancing rapidly from research prototypes to commercial products. Companies worldwide are investing billions to bring humanoids into manufacturing, logistics, healthcare and services. For Sweden, with its robotics heritage and world-leading industry, this is both an opportunity and a challenge.
 
The session combines a keynote, a live humanoid robot demonstration and a panel discussion. The keynote examines the technologies driving progress, the global momentum behind the field, and the key engineering and deployment challenges that remain. A moderated panel then brings together researchers in humanoid robotics and production automation alongside industry representatives to explore: Are industry and society ready for humanoids? What can we realistically expect in the near term? And what must Sweden do to punch above its weight and put itself on the map in physical AI and humanoid robotics?

content.title: AI, Talent and Innovation: Can Sweden stay competitive without India?
content.description: As AI transforms the global economy, countries are competing for talent, innovation and technological leadership at an unprecedented scale. For Sweden, this raises new questions about how international partnerships will shape future competitiveness — and what role India could play.
content.extendedDescription:
AI is rapidly reshaping economies, industries and global power structures. As competition for talent, technology and innovation accelerates, countries like Sweden — with strong research and innovation ecosystems — face growing pressure to strengthen their international position.

At the same time, India is emerging as a global AI powerhouse through major investments in digital infrastructure, entrepreneurship, research and technology talent. This creates new opportunities — but also strategic questions — for countries seeking to remain competitive.

Following recent initiatives launched during the Indian Prime Minister’s visit to Gothenburg, this panel explores how collaboration between Sweden and India could contribute to future research, innovation and industrial development.

The discussion will examine opportunities in research collaboration, talent exchange and industrial innovation — and how Sweden should position itself in a rapidly changing global AI landscape.

content.title: How can Europe create its own social media platform that serves democracy?
content.description: Social media shape opinion, spread disinformation and store data without democratic scrutiny, but also provide a platform for spreading democracy. Is it time for Europe to create its own social media platform, and what would success require?
content.extendedDescription:
Democracy is being challenged from within by platforms built for engagement rather than truth. Polarisation increases, facts are relativised and citizens' data are controlled by actors without European roots. Meanwhile, opportunities are growing to build alternatives grounded in European values of privacy, transparency and freedom of expression.

How does today's platform logic affect democratic debate? What do regulation, technology and civil society need to reverse the trend? What role can Europe take? Is it time for its own social media platform?

content.title: How can trade associations better support their members?
content.description: Small businesses create the most new jobs. They are the largest taxpayers in 9 out of 10 municipalities. Yet many important sectors lack the resources to make their voices heard. How can we change this?
content.extendedDescription:
Many trade associations do fantastic work but often lack the time, resources or right contacts to pursue advocacy fully. This is precisely why Företagarna Branschpartner exists. We bring together associations that want to be stronger together and create direct dialogue with politicians and decision-makers. Through our networks and policy experts, we give your voice greater impact on critical issues such as the business climate, red tape, skills supply and employment law.

Thomas Byström, who leads Företagarna Branschpartner, will be present to explain this work.

SVEBRA has already joined us to maximise its influence. Would you like to do the same? During Almedalsveckan, Tuesday–Thursday, Företagarna will be at SVEBRA's Beredskapscafé. We welcome meetings with trade associations wanting closer access to decision-makers and a stronger position. Are you in Almedalen? Contact us directly to arrange a meeting and explore how we can work together to become stronger!

content.title: Why does it take five years to build a charging site?
content.description: The will to make the transition exists, but bureaucracy is holding it back. Three years to obtain permission to build a charging site. content.title: Healthcare cannot do everything – who should decide, and how do we talk about it?
content.description: Healthcare has limited resources, both staff and money, and cannot meet every citizen's needs or wishes. Who should take responsibility for deciding what publicly funded healthcare should include, and how should we talk to citizens about those limits?
content.extendedDescription:
Politicians are accused of being unable to set limits on healthcare; the knowledge-based management system and public agencies produce guidelines seen as driving resource use; and professionals try to do the best for their patients, while we know healthcare resources are limited. How do we navigate this difficult equation?

In Västra Götalandsregionen, politicians have decided to work systematically on priority-setting across different areas of care, testing models to address growing expectations of healthcare provision from different quarters. Could this provide a starting point for better dialogue with citizens about what they should be able to expect from healthcare given resource constraints? At the seminar, representatives of regional politics, healthcare management, public agencies, the national knowledge-based management structure and the medical profession discuss who is responsible for deciding healthcare's limits and how to talk about them with citizens.

content.title: The weakest link: how does inadequate infrastructure threaten industry and Sweden's competitiveness?
content.description: Is Sweden's transport infrastructure equipped to meet both industry's needs and the new security situation's demands for robustness, redundancy and preparedness? When business competitiveness, society's ability to maintain supplies and the needs of total defence converge in the same transport system, new perspectives are required.
content.extendedDescription:
When transport stops: is Swedish infrastructure built for the new security situation?
Infrastructure is no longer just about costs per kilometre and logistics – it is a matter of national resilience, business-critical robustness and regional survival. In a changed international environment, the Swedish transport system faces entirely new demands. Yet we often still plan and make decisions in silos.
This seminar takes a wider view, analysing the transport system as an interconnected whole, with a focus on the strategic E12 corridor and Västerbotniabanan.
The overall perspective that is often forgotten: from Helsinki to the nearest Atlantic port, the fastest and most strategic route follows the E12 corridor – through Finland, across Kvarken and on through Västerbotten to Mo i Rana. This makes E12 a key corridor for both civilian and military transport in northern Europe.
Main themes:
• The strategic east-west corridor and local growth
• Preparedness, supplies and industrial vulnerability
• From vulnerability to systems thinking

content.title: Sweden wants to become a leading AI nation, but who is preparing young people to drive that development?
content.description: AI is changing working life faster than the education system is changing. How can we prepare young people for long working lives in an era when technology, vocational skills, responsibility, judgement and personal maturity must interact? What role does vocational education play in Sweden's future supply of skills?
content.extendedDescription:
Sweden wants to become a leading AI nation, while many young people face a rapidly changing labour market and growing uncertainty about which educational choices are truly future-proof. This seminar shifts the focus from whether schools should use AI to the more fundamental question of the people Sweden needs to nurture for long working lives in which technology and human abilities must work together.

The seminar particularly highlights vocational education's role in the future supply of skills. What do employers need as technology becomes smarter? How can schools prepare young people for jobs that have yet to be fully defined? And what must policymakers enable so that education better matches a working life in which digital readiness, responsibility, judgement, teamwork and vocational skills become increasingly important? By bringing together perspectives from education, working life and society, we create a constructive discussion about confidence in the future, relevance and young people's entry into employment.
content.subject: Education

content.title: Who draws the healthcare map – politicians or companies?
content.description: Consolidation in the private health and social care sector affects how care is organised, how investments are made and how patients encounter healthcare. But how well is the political debate keeping up as the market changes?
content.extendedDescription:
Join a breakfast seminar where Grant Thornton presents its new report on privatisation, consolidation and ownership models in health and social care. This is followed by a moderated discussion with specially invited guests from the sector about the consequences of these developments – and how political decisions, regulation of private providers and governance, deliberately or otherwise, help shape the market. What is a desirable balance between small providers whose owners are close to patients or service users and larger providers with greater resources, who may be more equal counterparts for a region or municipality?

Among other issues, we discuss the clearest current trends, how governance models and regulations affect ownership, operating models and market structure, and what these developments mean for equity, quality and long-term capacity.

The discussion is followed by networking.

content.title: Hijabs on children – freedom or oppression?
content.description: Honour-related oppression is a widespread societal problem in which controlling women's and girls' sexuality is central. The hijab is a tool for placing responsibility for men's sexual behaviour on girls and women – and putting hijabs on children sexualises young girls' bodies.
content.extendedDescription:
Honour-related oppression is a widespread societal problem practised within religious and cultural value systems in which controlling women's and girls' sexuality is central. The hijab is a tool that sexualises young girls' bodies, deprives women of the right to decide over their own bodies, and symbolises women's and girls' responsibility for men's sexual behaviour.

This panel discussion addresses the role of the hijab in a culture of honour and its contested role in Swedish society, focusing on girls under the age of majority. We discuss the background to the hijab's role in an honour context, freedom of expression, freedom of religion and whether the hijab is compatible with schools' gender equality mission.

Devin Rexvid, a researcher on honour-related violence and oppression, opens with an introduction to the hijab's role and significance within honour culture, voluntary choice, and the consequences for girls and women who do not wear a hijab.

Can we speak of voluntary choice when discussing the hijab?

content.title: The bank of the future – who will finance the next generation of entrepreneurs?
content.description: Swedish small and medium-sized businesses account for more than half of GDP and four out of five new jobs. Yet many business owners report increasing difficulty accessing capital. Has the banking system become a brake on growth for Swedish businesses? Does today's credit policy put the next generation of entrepreneurs at risk?
content.extendedDescription:
Today's banking system favours large, established companies, while growing businesses find it increasingly difficult to access capital. Specialist banks, fintech and data-driven credit models open up new opportunities for Swedish growth companies. How can we ensure that the Swedish businesses of the future have access to capital to grow, invest and create jobs? What roles should major banks, investors and new entrants play in future financing? Has the banking system become a brake on Swedish businesses? Are today's credit models still designed for an industrial society rather than entrepreneurial businesses? Does Sweden need a new banking system for entrepreneurs? How can we build a financing system that strengthens competitiveness and the Swedish businesses of the future?
In one of Almedalen's most topical economic discussions, entrepreneurs, investors, major banks and challengers meet to discuss whether today's banking system is holding back Swedish competitiveness and who will finance tomorrow's businesses.

content.title: Healthcare on equal terms: how do we get there?
content.description: Since 1982, the Health and Medical Services Act has required care on equal terms, yet major differences remain. The causes are complex and interconnected. Fundamentally, this is an ethical issue of fairness, responsibility and priorities.
content.extendedDescription:
The law requires care on equal terms, yet substantial differences remain. How society treats its most vulnerable people, those unable to navigate the system, living far from care or unable to understand the language, reveals the values guiding it beyond legislation and election promises.

These differences are well documented. Socioeconomically disadvantaged groups use less care relative to their needs. Geographical differences persist between rural areas and cities, while digitalisation improves access for some but excludes others.

These factors reinforce one another: location determines access, socioeconomic status affects the ability to navigate the system, and resource shortages hit some groups harder.

What is needed to make the law's objective a reality? There are no simple answers, but ethical choices must be made about governance, priorities and responsibility. We discuss what it actually takes to move closer to the goal.

content.title: Sweden spends hundreds of billions on healthcare, but almost nothing on keeping people healthy
content.description: Can private healthcare providers ensure Sweden shifts to preventive care and becomes a world leader in longevity?
content.extendedDescription:
We spend almost SEK 700 billion annually on healthcare in Sweden, yet we are not becoming healthier. The Swedish system is built to treat disease rather than prevent it. Meanwhile, we know that up to 80 per cent of the healthcare burden comes from lifestyle diseases: conditions we can substantially influence ourselves.
The average Swede spends the last ten years of life in impaired health. Reducing that period offers major societal gains.
With the report ‘From Medical Care to Health Care – How Longevity Strengthens Public Health and the Economy’, we propose shifting from ‘How do we treat disease?’ to ‘How do we keep people healthy for as long as possible?’.

content.title: What will Stockholm's residents eat then?
content.description: Stockholm is one of Europe's fastest-growing metropolitan regions, but also one of the most dependent. We have built a system that is extremely efficient in everyday life but potentially fragile in a crisis. Who is actually responsible for ensuring Stockholm's residents have food on their plates?
content.extendedDescription: The Stockholm region has a clear imbalance: high consumption, low local production and heavy dependence on long national and global supply chains. Meanwhile, pressure on agricultural land grows as the city expands and competition for land, resources and infrastructure intensifies. At its heart, this is also about the relationship between city and countryside: how metropolitan needs, growth and consumption connect to conditions for Swedish production, farming and food supplies nationwide. During the seminar, a panel discusses questions such as: where are the vulnerabilities? Who is responsible? What is needed to create a food system in which city and countryside strengthen one another, and how can responsibility be monitored and rewarded in practice?

content.title: Are AI and entrepreneurship Sweden's next growth engine?
content.description: AI is already changing how companies create value, how new business models emerge and how new companies are formed. Meanwhile, a global race for talent, investment and innovation in AI is under way. Sweden is well placed to take a leading position – but what will it take?
content.extendedDescription:
AI is already changing how companies create value, develop products and reach their customers. But AI is also changing the very conditions for entrepreneurship. What previously required large teams, substantial capital and long development cycles can now be achieved by small, agile companies using AI. New business models are emerging, barriers to innovation are falling and the opportunities to build global companies from a local base are greater than ever.

History shows that regions that succeed early in combining new technology with strong entrepreneurship often become tomorrow's growth engines. The question is whether Sweden and cities such as Gothenburg are ready to take that position in the AI era. Competition is fierce. Cities and regions across the Nordic countries and Europe are investing to attract companies, skills and capital.

Has AI Gothenburg cracked the code for creating these conditions?
- In less than 4 weeks, more than 100 AI companies have applied to be part of the initiative!
What are the ingredients needed?

content.title: Circularity – how hard can it be?
content.description: Europe faces a transition towards more resource-efficient ways of doing business. For several reasons, this transition has become increasingly urgent. Why is circularity both necessary and difficult? What is needed to move from principle to practice?
content.extendedDescription:
In a short time, securing access to materials and components has become a matter of both security and competitiveness. In addition, demands to reduce carbon footprints and preserve biodiversity are increasing. Working with circular principles is an effective way to meet all these challenges.
Circularity often sounds obvious: use resources more intelligently, recycle more, repair, reuse and design products to last. But for manufacturing companies, it is rarely that simple in practice.
The transition affects the entire business: product design, material choices, supply chains, servicing, spare parts, take-back, data, customer requirements, regulations and new business models. At every stage, practical questions need to be resolved. Can the product be refurbished and sold again? Do the market, logistics and profitability exist? How do new technical requirements, standards and regulations affect the ability to reuse products? What sounds simple in theory quickly becomes more complex in reality.
content.subject: Sustainability

content.title: Pitch on a Rib – who gets to meet investors?
content.description: Access to investors determines which ideas become reality, but networks and geography often determine who even gets through the door. Do the meeting place and format affect which companies obtain funding? And what is needed for more entrepreneurs to reach capital?
content.extendedDescription:
While the rest of Almedalen sits in seminar rooms, we cast off in a RIB from Visby Hamn. On board: a hand-picked line-up of startups, sharp investors and Gotland's coast as the backdrop.

No spotlights, no slide decks. Just innovative ideas and people who can help bring them to life.

We head out to sea at full speed, pitch in front of one of Gotland's highest and most dramatic cliffs, then return to the harbour. The rest happens on the jetty.

While the RIB is out, the boathouse at the harbour is open for mingling: coffee, sea air and the people building and investing on Gotland. Come ashore and stay for the conversations.

By moving the meeting from the seminar room to the sea, we want to lower the barrier between ideas and capital and show that the best conversations do not always happen where you expect.

content.title: From funding gap to growth engine: how do we advance Swedish medtech?
content.description: Swedish medtech has great potential but is held back by funding gaps between validated innovation and implementation for customers and patients. What does the sector need to become a stronger engine of growth?
content.extendedDescription:
Swedish medtech has the potential to become a stronger growth engine for healthcare, exports and regional development. Yet many companies face significant funding gaps between validated innovation and implementation in healthcare.

At this seminar, Medeon Science Park, Smile Venture Hub and Invest in Skåne present findings from a preliminary study funded by Tillväxtverket. Based on interviews with startups, scaleups, established companies and investors, it examines today's funding landscape and the challenges facing companies at different stages of growth.

We also present a new report on MedTech in Skåne produced by Regional Utveckling Skåne together with Invest in Skåne.

The seminar concludes with a panel of business representatives, investors and innovation system stakeholders discussing how to strengthen Swedish medtech and improve companies' opportunities to grow, attract capital and bring innovations to healthcare and patients.

content.title: Who staffs Sweden's security services? Skills provision, wage formation and the state's responsibility as an employer
content.description: Sweden is strengthening its defences, but skills provision risks becoming the major bottleneck. How can the state recruit, develop and retain staff in the police, armed forces, customs and coast guard when competition for workers increases and security requirements tighten?
content.extendedDescription:
Sweden is strengthening its defence, expanding the police and placing higher demands on agencies responsible for border protection and preparedness. Yet many organisations report difficulties recruiting, developing and retaining the right expertise. In professions where skills develop through education, experience and long-term knowledge transfer, staff shortages can directly affect society's security and resilience.

The discussion starts from how the state can secure long-term staffing and skills in the police, armed forces, customs and coast guard. We discuss the challenges, how state employer policy affects the ability to attract and retain qualified staff, and the role of wage formation, working conditions and career paths in operational capability.

The seminar is a panel discussion with representatives from politics, research and the professions concerned.

content.title: How do we secure tomorrow's drinking water when systems are put to the test?
content.description: We take water for granted until it is unavailable. Climate change, water scarcity and increased preparedness requirements place new demands on Sweden's water supply. In many places, the focus has shifted from capacity shortages to whether enough raw water exists to produce drinking water.
content.extendedDescription:
Society must manage both everyday challenges and major disruptions. How do we secure access to clean water as conditions change?

In this seminar, experts from the water sector, public services and business discuss future water supplies. The conversation starts from current issues of climate change, water scarcity, preparedness and societal vulnerability, as well as emerging solutions.

How well equipped are our systems today? What can we learn from Gotland's work on water? What role can new technologies play, and how do we create a water supply that works both in everyday life and when society is under pressure?

Topics include water preparedness, climate adaptation and societal vulnerability, and how solutions such as desalination, water reuse and mobile water treatment plants can contribute to more secure supplies.

content.title: How do we develop our environments without losing architectural and cultural heritage values?
content.description: Visby and the visible and hidden layers of its cultural environment. How is a city shaped by its history, and how does each generation rewrite it? As Swedish city centres change, we face the same question: how do we develop our shared environments without losing the values that make them significant?
content.extendedDescription:
Visby's squares and public spaces contain both visible and hidden layers of stories. During this guided city walk, organised by Gotlands Museum and Tengbom, we explore how the city's cultural environment has changed over the centuries and how different generations have left their mark on urban space.

Among our stops is Donners plats, where we discuss how historical traces have developed, been reinterpreted and sometimes replaced as new needs and functions emerged. Change and additions to the urban environment are not new phenomena, but a process that has continued from the Middle Ages to today.

Through conversations while walking, we explore how cultural environments can remain vibrant and relevant while preserving their historic values. The walk invites reflection on how we understand, use and develop our shared environments, and which stories we choose to pass on to the future.

content.title: How do we find the courage for conversations that matter?
content.description: Important things are often said too late, or not at all. We frequently choose silence over discomfort, postponing, softening or avoiding conversations that matter. This affects trust, decisions and working conditions, but the price is rarely visible until it has already been paid.
content.extendedDescription:
We usually know what needs saying but avoid it for fear of conflict, discomfort or resistance. Some conversations never happen, are postponed or softened, or move to the corridor after the meeting. This roundtable stays with that issue. Share your experience and help shape how we dare to have conversations that matter: practically, simply, combining digital and physical participation.

We explore real workplace situations where people chose not to say what they thought. Together, we examine what stopped them, what could have been done differently and how to create more courage in everyday conversations.

You are a co-creator, not an audience member. Through participants' experiences and reflections, we create a shared guide to conversations we would rather avoid.

content.title: Technological sovereignty – how are Sweden and the EU preparing for their own security and defence capability?
content.description: Digital daily life in Sweden and Europe relies on global technology and infrastructure, often from the USA. In a heightened security situation, European technological sovereignty becomes a strategic issue.
content.extendedDescription:
Digital infrastructure is no longer simply a matter of innovation and competitiveness. Cloud services, operating systems, components and communications networks are essential to critical operations, preparedness and military capability. Meanwhile, Europe is heavily dependent on technology and infrastructure controlled by actors outside the EU.
What happens if access to key digital services is restricted? How vulnerable is Europe's digital ecosystem? Which dependencies are most critical from a defence and preparedness perspective? And how can Europe strengthen its technological freedom of action without isolating itself from global innovation?
Tre brings together decision-makers, security policy experts and business representatives to discuss technological sovereignty as a matter of security, defence capability, competitiveness and innovation capacity.

content.title: Information preparedness and communication in crisis and war
content.description: Who ensures communication and information in crisis and war? How do essential societal actors reach people when it matters most? How does the emergency alert chain work, and who picks up on what is happening? What can we expect in terms of psychological influence operations?
content.extendedDescription:
Communication is the most important thing under challenging conditions. In this session, essential societal actors discuss systematic security work, information preparedness and communication in crisis and war.

In an era marked by hybrid influence operations, cyber threats and uncertainty in our neighbourhood, what international developments do security companies need to prepare for to ensure security provision for companies and critical services?

SVT's total defence mission is to ensure the public can access news, public information and important announcements in everyday life, during crises, heightened alert and war. They share experiences of building resilience, securing information provision and strengthening public preparedness.

SOS Alarm discusses how the emergency alert chain works, what can go wrong and experiences from Ukraine.

SäkerhetsArenan is organised by SäkerhetsBranschen, Stöldskyddsföreningen, Brandskyddsföreningen, Tryggare Sverige, Säkerhetsföretagen, Företagsuniversitetet and SOFF.

content.title: What is really being said in the energy debate: plenty of talk, little customer focus?
content.description: Electricity support, high-cost protection, capacity charges, electricity taxes, congestion revenues and prices moving in every direction. The 2026 election year has brought many variables for electricity customers to navigate, yet they are rarely present when energy is discussed.
content.extendedDescription:
We offer a review of the energy debate during Almedalsveckan and what it could mean for Swedish electricity customers, the election campaign and the coming parliamentary term.

The political ambition to electrify Sweden places high demands on the electricity system. The way forward has been extensively debated in recent years, particularly here in Almedalen. Customers are often expected to play an important role by adjusting consumption and adapting to volatile, unpredictable prices. Sometimes they are compensated afterwards. What has the debate looked like during the 2026 election year and Almedalsveckan, and what could forthcoming decisions mean for customers? What do Swedish electricity customers want today, and how can the energy industry and politicians meet those needs?

content.title: Children's right to a dignified life is not measured in minutes
content.description: Children with disabilities are denied personal assistance to which they are entitled. Today's narrow rules hit the most vulnerable hard. We demand legislative changes so that the child's full needs count.
content.extendedDescription:
Visit RBU's outdoor stand at Almedalen and learn more about the Minuter campaign and why we demand changes to legislation for children and young people with disabilities.

This is not an exaggeration but is based on actual court rulings.
Try it, get involved and share your experience on social media with #rbukampanjminuter.

content.title: Megaregions as a political tool – shaping Sweden's and Europe's competitiveness
content.description: Sweden is experiencing a prolonged recession while its Nordic neighbours show stronger growth and capacity for transition. How can greater cross-border integration of labour markets, innovation and infrastructure strengthen competitiveness and create sustainable growth?
content.extendedDescription:
Global competition, geopolitical uncertainty and the green transition place new demands on European regions. Meanwhile, research, including from the Kiel Institute, shows that functional megaregions can play a crucial role in competitiveness, innovation and economic development.

Starting from the Oslo–Hamburg corridor, the seminar discusses how cross-border cooperation can strengthen Sweden's position in the Nordic region and Europe. How well do current governance, investment and support systems fit functional labour markets, innovation environments and transport corridors extending across national borders? What barriers impede development, and what political decisions are needed to unlock potential?

content.title: Parenthood on equal terms: how do we ensure all perspectives are included in fertility care?
content.description: Can today's fertility care meet different circumstances and needs? How do people with physical disabilities experience fertility care?
content.extendedDescription:
Although care should be based on individual psychosocial assessments, many people report being reduced to their diagnosis or disability and having their suitability as future parents questioned before an assessment has even been made. Their experiences raise questions about how well the current system recognises different life circumstances, and whether people with disabilities have equal opportunities to start a family.

In the report ‘She said: If you were my daughter, I would advise you to have an abortion’, Funktionsrätt Sverige and RFSU collect people with disabilities' experiences of fertility care.

How do we create fertility care that assesses people with disabilities on their individual circumstances rather than assumptions about them? Which perspectives do we need to understand better? And how can healthcare, public authorities and civil society work together to strengthen everyone's opportunities for parenthood?

Join a conversation about experience, knowledge and the path towards more equitable fertility care.

content.title: The state's blind spot: crisis communication in a privatised urban landscape
content.description: What do we do when mobile networks are overloaded and online rumours cause panic? Public authorities' plans clash with citizens' digital everyday lives. How can we bridge the gap between government and business, and secure public screens in the urban landscape as a crisis communication channel in modern total defence?
content.extendedDescription:
Government directives require a rapid expansion of total defence capability by using civilian and private infrastructure. Yet frameworks and incentives for cooperation between the state and private actors are currently lacking. With no preparedness requirements for commercial information displays, the state is missing out on a huge untapped resource for crisis communication.
This seminar addresses the need for a new public-private social contract. When disinformation spreads and analogue or digital information flows are blocked, physical screens in squares, transport hubs and public transport can serve as a critical crisis channel for verified information. JCDecaux invites public authorities, politicians and industry representatives to discuss the legal, technical and operational challenges of building a secure and immediate way to reach citizens in public spaces, before a crisis strikes.
content.subject: Communication/information

content.description: As geopolitical tensions rise, resistance under occupation is once again a relevant question. During the Cold War, Sweden had clear plans for continued resistance. What remains relevant today, and how should a democratic society prepare?
content.extendedDescription: A conversation about Sweden’s secret stay-behind network during the Cold War - the clandestine resistance structure prepared to operate in the event of Soviet occupation. content.title: How can Sweden attract the world's best startups – and enable them to stay?
content.description: Sweden competes globally for innovative companies, entrepreneurs and international talent. Yet both foreign founders and Swedish startups face barriers to establishment, residence permits and recruitment. What is needed for more people to choose to build and develop tomorrow's companies?
content.extendedDescription:
Sweden competes globally for innovative startups, entrepreneurs and international talent. Yet international founders and Swedish startups face barriers to establishment, residence permits, running a business and recruitment, risking lost investment, innovation and jobs.

Commissioned by Business Sweden under the government's Work in Sweden assignment, SISP has mapped these challenges. The work has produced a policy report and a national playbook to help innovation organisations better support international startups seeking to establish themselves in Sweden and international researchers wishing to commercialise their research here. The seminar presents the playbook for the first time, followed by a discussion of the changes needed to make Sweden more attractive to international startups and talent.

content.title: Time for Sweden to wake up if we are to benefit from the Fehmarn Belt link
content.description: When the Fehmarn Belt link opens, Europe's centre of gravity will move closer to Sweden. The challenge is to ensure infrastructure, business and tourism are equipped to seize the opportunities arising from greater accessibility and competition.
content.extendedDescription:
The Fehmarn Belt link is northern Europe's largest infrastructure investment. Together with other investments, such as the expansion of Copenhagen International Airport, it creates new opportunities for Swedish trade, investment, skills supply, tourism and international accessibility.

Fully benefiting from these new flows requires investment in Swedish infrastructure and transport capacity, and a clear national strategy. Although often viewed as a southern Swedish issue, it concerns the competitiveness of all Sweden and the Nordic region in a growing European corridor.

Drawing on a new scenario report, Visit Skåne and Malmö stad invite Visit Sweden and Visita to discuss how Sweden can prepare for increased flows. The focus is on destination development, tourism, accessibility, regional development and international competitiveness. Moderator Max Granström, Visit Skåne, presents the report and leads the discussion.

content.title: Security and climate preparedness in Swedish and EU ports
content.description: In March 2026, the European Commission adopted two strategies to promote competitiveness, sustainability, security and resilience in the EU's waterborne sector. They focus mainly on ports, shipping and shipbuilding, sectors crucial to EU trade, economic growth, security and defence.
content.extendedDescription:
Swedish ports play an important role in national transport, the economy and preparedness. Port regions need to increase their understanding of how climate change may affect them and strengthen their ability to consider new societal changes and geopolitical threats.

Ports now face several new and complex risks linked to the climate crisis, societal changes and geopolitical challenges. With these new strategies in place, EU member states, including Sweden, will be obliged to adopt strategic, feasible plans addressing and managing climate resilience.

content.title: Construction's hidden waste – can digitalisation cut materials, transport and emissions?
content.description: Construction accounts for a large share of Sweden's resource consumption. Much waste originates early: incorrect quantities, duplicate orders and unnecessary transport. How can digitalisation reduce waste and emissions, and what do smaller actors need to make the transition?
content.extendedDescription:
The discussion starts with a concrete question: how much material is wasted in construction, and where in the chain does this happen? Much waste and unnecessary transport between wholesalers and construction sites originates during quantity estimation and ordering, long before anything is built.
We discuss how digitalisation and AI can reduce material waste and transport, what wholesalers, installers and contractors need to change, and how the green transition can progress without raising costs for smaller actors.
The focus is on structural societal issues, not individual products or solutions.
content.subject: Sustainability

content.title: Sustainable construction in practice – from production to practice: how the construction industry is transitioning
content.description: Swedish construction and materials manufacturing play a crucial role in the climate transition, but how does this translate into practice? Supply chain transparency, climate requirements for materials and industry's ability to transition are crucial if the entire construction chain is to meet climate targets.
content.extendedDescription: This seminar focuses on industry's role in the climate transition. How can manufacturers reduce their products' climate footprint? What change – regulation, incentives or technology – would have the greatest effect right now? The seminar consists of short presentations by industry stakeholders followed by a moderated panel discussion with audience questions.

content.title: How have the parties performed on environmental policy, and what are they promising next?
content.description: Which parties have performed best and worst on environmental policy during the parliamentary term? How have the government and parliamentary parties acted on environmental issues in 2022-2026, and what are they promising for the next term?
content.extendedDescription:
Discuss environmental issues with our experts while charging your phone and trying Naturskyddsföreningen's election compass for climate and nature.

Naturskyddsföreningen is a politically independent nonprofit organisation with more than 200 000 members nationwide. We are deeply rooted in research, and our vision is a sustainable future on a healthy, living planet. Since 1985, we have scrutinised environmental policy ahead of parliamentary elections by sending a broad environmental policy questionnaire to the parliamentary parties and evaluating their actions during the preceding term.

We assess political parties in the same way, regardless of party affiliation. We believe that all political parties, wherever they sit on the political spectrum, should naturally work towards a stable climate, healthy ecosystems and a toxin-free environment.

Which issue will determine your vote? Visit our tent on Strandvägen and discuss the election for climate and nature!

content.title: Energy security as a competitive advantage – how can AI and geothermal energy strengthen Sweden's resilience?
content.description: Energy supply has become a strategic security issue. What role can geothermal energy play in Sweden's security and competitiveness, and what is needed to meet future electricity demand? How can digital technology accelerate progress?
content.extendedDescription:
Jordkraft Energy's pilot project with Naftogaz in Ukraine explores how geothermal electricity generation can strengthen resilience in a country whose critical infrastructure is under severe pressure. Meanwhile, global geothermal investment is increasing as AI, data centres and electrification drive rapidly growing demand for stable, fossil-free baseload power. Data, AI and digitalisation are crucial to scaling new energy sources by reducing risks, improving exploration efficiency and providing better evidence for investment decisions.

This seminar brings together representatives of energy, technology and investment to discuss geothermal energy's potential role in Sweden's security and competitiveness, what is needed to meet future electricity demand and how digital technology can accelerate progress.
content.subject: Energy
content.organizationType: Collaboration between different types of organisation

content.title: Parkinson's disease – the right treatment at the right time and the importance of physical activity
content.description: Parkinson's disease affects increasing numbers of people. In addition to medication, staying physically active is important. It is a central part of treatment for maintaining functions and training balance and reaction skills.
content.extendedDescription: We will provide information about Parkinson's disease and the importance of receiving the right treatment at the right time, with the right support over time. Together with the Arvsfonden-funded Pingis Parkinson project and Parkinson Gotland, we will offer politicians and the public information about how physical activity should be regarded as part of treatment. You can also try playing table tennis with us. We will present several proposals that can contribute to better public health, better care and treatment, greater knowledge in elderly care, and the application of sickness insurance, rules for sickness compensation and opportunities to participate in associations despite having a chronic illness.
content.subject: Health and social care

content.title: Preparing for tomorrow – Swedish defence investment in a new geopolitical context
content.description: Europe's security landscape has fundamentally changed. Several scenarios point to European NATO countries doubling defence investment in the near future. What regulatory measures are required? And how do we build for the long term in a sector expanding so dramatically in so little time?
content.extendedDescription:
Against this backdrop, we invite you to a breakfast seminar in Almedalen, bringing together leading global affairs analysts, investors and lawyers to examine developments from several perspectives.

The morning starts with an overview of global security and its implications for Europe and Sweden, followed by a closer look at how private equity views defence-sector opportunities: what drives investment interest and which factors are crucial to building attractive, sustainable long-term investment cases. The panel also addresses regulatory complexity, from investment to industrial transition, and offers practical insights into navigating a rapidly changing landscape.

content.title: From research to patients: how do we ensure innovation reaches patients in time?
content.description: How are research, clinical trials and patients' access to innovative treatments connected?
content.extendedDescription:
Sweden has long been a strong research nation, but many patients still have to wait for new treatments already used in other countries. How well do our decision-makers understand the connection between research, clinical trials, innovation and patients' access to treatment?

The seminar presents results from a new Novus survey of national, regional and municipal politicians. It examines knowledge of how innovative treatments are introduced into Swedish healthcare, the barriers to rapid implementation and the effects on Sweden's ability to attract research and clinical trials.

Drawing on the results, we bring together politicians and other key stakeholders to discuss strengthening the entire chain, from research and clinical studies to equitable, timely patient access.

The seminar is organised by Blodcancerforum in cooperation with AbbVie, Bristol Myers Squibb (BMS), Gilead, GSK, Johnson & Johnson and Roche.

content.title: The US has the billions, China the data – Can Small Giants save Swedish AI?
content.description: The US pours in endless venture capital and China has endless data. In Europe, we build regulations. Sweden will never win the AI war on the superpowers' terms. But what if our limitations are our greatest strength? How do we secure Swedish competitiveness by playing a completely different game?
content.extendedDescription:
Panel discussion, morning coffee & a classic Swedish breakfast sandwich ("frukostmacka").

While tech giants burn billions on supercomputers, AI is rewriting the rules of entrepreneurship. Today, a team of 1-3 people in Visby or Malmö, backed by AI agents, can do what used to take 500 employees in Silicon Valley.

We call them "Small Giants" – extremely capital-lean, resourceful companies that outmaneuver the giants through speed and creativity, rather than brute force.

We throw the old VC-hungry "unicorn" model in the trash to discuss how Swedish entrepreneurs can build global companies from day one.

In the panel we discuss: 
• Why Europe's AI strategy often misses the mark. 
• From Unicorn to Small Giant: Lowering the barrier to building global companies. 
• AI-native ways of working: How agents crush resource-rich competitors. 
• What Sweden's government and ecosystem must do now to accelerate these Small Giants.

content.title: Quality, knowledge and greater well-being in nursing care through quality registries
content.description: Behavioural and psychological symptoms of dementia (BPSD) reduce well-being and affect almost everyone with a cognitive disorder or dementia at some point during their illness. Can person-centred care interventions, multidisciplinary teamwork and a structured approach improve the person's well-being?
content.extendedDescription:
BPSD-registret is a national quality registry intended to ensure the quality of care for people with cognitive disorders or dementia.
Through person-centred care, BPSD-registret contributes to greater well-being and quality of life by reducing the person's behavioural and psychological symptoms of dementia, BPSD.
Regular, ongoing recording allows results to be monitored at individual level and aggregated at unit, municipal, county and national level. Individual results are used to improve each person's well-being. Aggregated data are used in research and improvement work to ensure quality and develop care and services. BPSD-registret also contributes to better multidisciplinary teamwork and opportunities for learning and reflection, increasing knowledge and care quality.

Across Sweden, services in this field use BPSD-registret to improve both care quality and staff knowledge.

content.title: Time passes, but Alzheimer's disease remains
content.description: Alzheimer's disease should be treated like other diseases. In January 2025, the Minister for Older People and Social Security tasked Vård- och omsorgsanalys with investigating whether knowledge and experience from cancer care could strengthen health and social care for people with dementia.
content.extendedDescription:
Alzheimer's disease is not part of natural ageing. It develops when nerve cells in the brain degenerate because harmful proteins have accumulated over a long period. For those affected, and particularly their families, Alzheimer's is a cruel disease. Watching a life partner, sibling, parent or friend slowly disappear is profoundly difficult. The disease also creates many questions and uncertainties for patients and relatives. People affected by Alzheimer's want clear guidance, a care plan and access to knowledge, just as with other serious diseases.

New methods of detection and diagnosis have enabled more people to receive a diagnosis earlier in the disease's course. This also means more people may live with an Alzheimer's diagnosis for longer without developing severe symptoms. A confirmed diagnosis also improves the conditions for person-centred health and social care throughout the disease
content.subject: Health and social care

content.title: The 2026 US midterm elections – what do they mean for Sweden and the global economy?
content.description: President Trump's approval ratings are at historic lows, and suddenly even Texas is in play. The 2026 US midterm elections could reshape the balance in Congress, the global economy and Swedish export industry. What would a shift in power mean?
content.extendedDescription:
Reform Society takes a deep dive into the US midterm elections together with Matt McMillan, an award-winning international political consultant and campaign strategist with experience from national elections in more than 40 countries and hundreds of congressional, senate and state-level races.

We look in particular at the senate race in Texas, where the Democrats' James Talarico – a teacher and theologian who frames progressive politics in Christian terms – faces the Trump-backed and controversial Ken Paxton. What would a shift of power in Congress mean for the US and for Sweden?

The format is an informal but well-informed on-stage conversation with plenty of room for questions, input and discussion from the audience.

content.title: Human trafficking in Sweden in 2026 — have we become better at protecting the most vulnerable?
content.description: Human trafficking is one of the most serious human rights violations of our time. Despite legislation, public-authority and international commitments, women, children and men continue to be subjected to sexual exploitation, forced labour, begging and other forms of exploitation. What action is needed, and by whom?
content.extendedDescription:
No single organisation can bear the responsibility for combating human trafficking alone. Effective action requires cooperation between public authorities, the justice system, civil society, churches and international organisations. How can this cooperation be strengthened? What experience do those who meet victims have? And what reforms are needed for Sweden to better prevent human trafficking, protect vulnerable people and hold perpetrators accountable?

Led by Erik Eckerdal, Bishop of Visby Diocese and Svenska kyrkan i utlandet (SKUT), representatives from the government, public authorities, churches and civil society come together to discuss human trafficking, prostitution, digital exploitation and Sweden's responsibility to safeguard the human dignity of the most vulnerable.

content.title: Autonomous vehicles – will Europe lead or fall behind?
content.description: Autonomous vehicles are no longer a future vision: they already operate commercially in the United States and China. Europe has the potential to lead but risks falling behind, not because technology is lacking but because regulations cannot keep up. How can we ensure operations centred on safety and accessibility?
content.extendedDescription:
Waymo makes more than 450,000 trips a week in the United States and Baidu over 250,000 in China. Europe has 35 pilot projects but few commercial routes. The market is expected to reach 44 billion euros by 2030, but only if Europe moves from pilots to actual deployment.
In an on-stage conversation, Vivetha Natterjee, Head of Autonomous Product & Deployment at Bolt, shares her assessment of the technology and industry today and what Europe needs to proceed on its own terms: harmonised regulation, Vision Zero as an ethical foundation and inclusion from day one.
Mattias Goldmann from 2030-sekretariatet leads the discussion, with audience questions and participation. Key themes include regulatory challenges, where a vehicle approved in Hamburg still cannot operate in Helsinki, road safety and how autonomous vehicles can enable accessible mobility for older people, people with disabilities and rural residents. What is needed so Sweden and Europe do not miss this opportunity?
content.subject: Sustainability

content.title:
Can Sweden afford to ignore women's health?
Growth, innovation and health – overlooked billions
content.description: Delayed diagnoses, lower quality of life, lost working years, missed business opportunities. Despite women making up half the population, major disparities remain in research, innovation, diagnostics and care. The consequences affect not only individuals but also productivity, the labour market and the economy.
content.extendedDescription:
Internationally, recognition is growing that women's health is not only a healthcare issue but also one of innovation, competitiveness and economic development. Meanwhile, research shows that many diseases disproportionately affecting women remain underrepresented in research, diagnostics and innovation. International analyses also indicate significant economic gains from narrowing the health gap between women and men.
Are innovations lacking, or the ability to implement them? Who is responsible for turning research into patient benefits, growth, jobs and exports?
A challenging discussion about women's health as the next major issue for growth, innovation, implementation and policy. Patient perspectives, startups, the pharmaceutical industry, the regional innovation system and politics come together to discuss what is needed to move from insight to action.
The seminar takes the form of a moderated conversation and panel, followed by audience questions if time permits.

content.title: Nordic Connector – how can we move from vision to reality?
content.description: Nordic Connector, a fixed link across Kvarken between Vasa and Umeå, would strengthen infrastructure redundancy, connect labour markets and create a new strategic east–west corridor for industry and trade. But how can we move from vision to reality?
content.extendedDescription:
In a heightened geopolitical situation, robust transport systems are crucial for security, supply and competitiveness. Connecting Sweden, Norway and Finland in the north shortens distances, expands labour markets and strengthens supply chains in an increasingly strategic region. The result is a stronger Nordic whole and a more competitive economy at a time of growing demands for security and cooperation.
Nordic Connector, a fixed link across Kvarken between Vasa and Umeå, would strengthen infrastructure redundancy, connect labour markets and create a new east–west corridor for industry and trade. But the project requires coordination, clear political priorities and new financing solutions.
How can we move from vision to reality and enable construction to begin on one of the Nordic region's most strategically significant infrastructure projects in modern times? During Almedalsveckan, we bring stakeholders together to discuss what is needed to move from idea to construction.
content.subject: Infrastructure/transport

content.title: What does it take to succeed with AI?
content.description: AI is often described as the solution. In practice, however, it functions more like a stress test for organisations. If leadership, culture and governance are lacking, AI becomes an amplifier of existing problems rather than a shortcut forward. So what does success require?
content.extendedDescription:
Using practical cases and experiences from the public and private sectors, the seminar addresses one of today's most decisive questions: why some succeed in turning AI into concrete change while others get stuck in pilot projects, fragmented initiatives and a lack of results. We discuss what it takes to build real implementation capacity, what conditions must be in place, what the path from pilot to scale can look like and which pitfalls risk slowing progress.

You will leave with a clearer picture of why those who start first or invest most are not always the ones who succeed with AI.

Coffee will be available during the seminar.

content.title: Basketball meets the city – how a basketball court became a community plan in Stockholm
content.description: How can cities, associations and businesses jointly strengthen participation, inclusion and hope for the future among children and young people? Basketball is Stockholm's second-largest team sport and an important meeting place. What can stakeholders learn from one another to create lasting value beyond sport?
content.extendedDescription:
The seminar discusses how basketball, municipalities and other stakeholders can work together to create lasting positive effects for children and young people. Drawing on concrete experience from Stockholm, we explore how local meeting places, associations and cooperation can strengthen safety, community and social sustainability.

The discussion starts from a unique three-year partnership between Stockholms stad and Svenska Basketbollförbundet, using basketball to drive participation, strengthen communities and develop new forms of cooperation between the public sector, associations and business.

We also discuss how major international sporting events can catalyse societal development and create value long after the matches end. How can investment in sport, meeting places and cooperation contribute to a cohesive city beyond the final whistle?

content.title: Customer insights as a competitive advantage
content.description: How do companies use AI to turn customer insights into action that actually drives growth for Swedish businesses?
content.extendedDescription:
Organisations hold more customer data than ever, but does this automatically lead to better decisions? Despite extensive investments in customer experience, research shows that almost 80 per cent of organisations believe they meet customers' expectations, while only 20 per cent of customers agree. This Experience Gap offers the greatest opportunities for growth and competitive advantage.

How do you move from data to action? How can AI and modern analytical tools help organisations understand what customers actually need? During the seminar, we share concrete examples and methods for making customer insights a strategic asset, and examine how to break down organisational silos, make insights available to more people and ensure the customer's voice becomes a natural part of decision-making.

The seminar also takes place on 24/6 at 11.00.

content.title: Sweden has its antibiotic factory – but who secures the rest?
content.description: Sweden has invested in domestic antibiotic manufacturing, but preparedness concerns the entire supply chain. Today, Europe has only one fully integrated antibiotic production chain, while active ingredients are imported from Asia. What is needed for a resilient antibiotic supply in the EU?
content.extendedDescription: Sweden has taken a historic step by investing in domestic antibiotic manufacturing. This is a welcome decision and reflects a broader shift in the approach to pharmaceutical preparedness. But preparedness concerns the entire supply chain, not a single factory. Today, more than 85% of all active pharmaceutical ingredients, known as APIs, are produced in China and India. Across Europe, there is only one fully integrated penicillin production chain, from active ingredient to finished product. One factory on an entire continent. No active ingredient, no antibiotics. Meanwhile, a government inquiry into medicine shortages and preparedness is under way, and strategic autonomy has grown from a health policy issue into a security policy issue. What political and structural conditions are needed to secure a resilient antibiotic supply in Sweden and Europe? Join a discussion on responsibility, preparedness and sustainable access to antibiotics, one of healthcare's most fundamental medicines.

content.title: Lowering food prices without compromising quality
content.description: How do we lower food prices without compromising quality? Despite reduced food VAT, global conditions risk continuing to drive up food supply chain costs.
content.extendedDescription:
How do we lower food prices without compromising quality, sustainability ambitions or Sweden's food preparedness? The government's food VAT reduction has brought welcome price cuts, but in an unsettled world with rising costs for inputs, transport and energy, efforts to reduce prices must continue. Coop has therefore developed proposals to simplify rules and remove administrative requirements, reducing costs without compromising quality or sustainability.

Together with politicians and food supply chain stakeholders, we open a constructive, solution-oriented discussion of these proposals and other measures for lower food prices, aiming to preserve consumer protection, food safety and sustainability initiatives. Alongside the seminar, Coop launches a report proposing how to move from words to action on simpler rules.

content.title: Fewer barriers, more business owners: how do we get there?
content.description: Is Sweden a good country in which to start a business? We would like to think so, but reality tells a different story. Why are fewer people choosing to take the plunge? What happens to jobs and public services when entrepreneurship declines? Most importantly, what can we do to reverse the trend?
content.extendedDescription:
Since the turn of the millennium, the number of business owners increased by 110 000, but over the past two years it has fallen by 15 000. The business owner community is not only shrinking; it is also ageing and remains strikingly homogeneous. The share of business owners aged between 65 and 74 is growing, and only 28.9 per cent are women, one of the lowest proportions in Europe.
Conditions are tough for those who do run businesses. Företagarna's Småföretagsbarometern 2025 report shows the worst economic conditions for small businesses in 40 years. One in five business owners struggles to make ends meet. Investments are postponed or cancelled altogether.
This is not a temporary downturn we can simply wait out. Sweden is falling behind in the prosperity rankings. The growth crisis is more acute than it appears, because every krona of tax revenue must be generated before it can be redistributed. Without growing businesses, the tax base shrinks, and with it the public services we take for granted.

content.title: AI, trust and everyday life
content.description: AI is changing how we work, make decisions and interact with people. But how do we build trust, engagement and real change when technology develops faster than people's habits and behaviours?
content.extendedDescription:
AI can change a great deal: how we work, make decisions and interact with people. But one thing stays the same: trust still starts with a hello.

As technology becomes more advanced, the human dimension becomes more important, not less.

This conversation brings together Linda Vikström, Communications Director at IKEA Sverige, and Johanna Friman, brand expert at Doings. The discussion is organised by Doings and Kinbergs Plats 3. Together, they explore how trust is built when technology and ways of working change.

Drawing on IKEA's and Doings' work to bring about behavioural change in organisations, they discuss leadership, culture, trust and behaviour close to people's everyday lives.

The conversation is moderated by Marcus Wärn.

You will take away:
• How trust affects change in the AI era
• How people and behaviours determine whether change succeeds
• Perspectives from IKEA and Doings
• What leadership and communication need to do when technology develops rapidly

content.title: Indigenous rights, a mining nation and polarisation – can human rights guide the climate transition?
content.description: As Sweden transitions, conflicts over land, resources and influence are growing. Can human rights and Indigenous rights create clearer rules for mining, energy and the climate transition? How can we bring more nuance to conflicting objectives, and what is the way forward?
content.extendedDescription:
The debate in Sweden about the rights of the Sámi people is polarised. Political statements describe Sámi culture as an obstacle to societal development. At the same time, international criticism and protests continue over the state's handling of Sámi rights to influence and land. Indigenous rights are rendered invisible in many of the decisions that affect Sámi rights the most.

The Sámi are among the first to experience the effects of the climate crisis and have long advocated the urgent need for a transition. How can human rights contribute to clarity and understanding in the decision-making processes surrounding mines, wind power and other land use? Why must the state and companies treat the Sámi people as part of the solution?

content.title: How can we enable more industrial projects that benefit both the climate and national security?
content.description: New technology reduces CO2 emissions and improves security of supply by producing synthetic fuels when electrified lime production, essential for high-quality steelmaking, captures unavoidable CO2 emissions. Cooperation between the private and public sectors makes this possible.
content.extendedDescription:
When energy and fuel are strategic vulnerabilities, central government, municipalities and business must cooperate to enable green investment that strengthens industrial robustness. Our neighbouring countries attract investment with faster decisions on electricity, permits and state involvement. For more investments to materialise in Sweden, we must improve our transition support systems, including Klimatklivet and Industriklivet.
In this panel discussion, private and public sector representatives discuss the need for cooperation and possible improvements. We highlight an example in which electrified lime production separates carbon dioxide from the lime reaction into a controlled stream, enabling steel production using essential lime with significantly lower CO2 emissions. These emissions instead become synthetic fuels, using electricity, hydrogen and carbon dioxide, contributing to lower emissions and greater security of supply.

content.title: The transport sector: a backbone of total defence
content.description: Which interests need to coexist and work together for greater resilience? How does the transport sector function, and how can robust infrastructure be secured as a strategic security issue in everyday life, in a crisis and, in the worst case, in war?
content.extendedDescription:
This concerns the principles that need to be considered in transport, including people's lives and health; the functioning of society, for example food and business transport; commuting; the environment and economic assets; and national sovereignty, transit and host nation support.
Sweden must never come to a standstill. To fully succeed, public agencies and business now need to deepen their cooperation.

The seminar will focus on three perspectives on the principles that need to be considered in transport:
• Normal conditions: What must already be in place when we build and plan infrastructure to meet several interests at once?
• The crisis perspective: What must work from each actor's perspective when the system is severely tested?
• Prioritisation in an actual crisis: What is the order of priorities? How do we balance different interests and ensure shared priorities in a real emergency?

The seminar will also be streamed online; this page will be updated with a link.
content.subject: Infrastructure/transport

content.title: As the world rearms – how do we build lasting peace and security?
content.description: How can diplomacy, peacebuilding and military capability together contribute to long-term security? And what role does Sweden play in preventing conflicts and strengthening peace in an increasingly uncertain world? What does security mean today in 2026, and what matters most for Sweden?
content.extendedDescription:
Europe is undergoing its largest military build-up since the Cold War. The war in Ukraine, conflicts in the Middle East and growing geopolitical tensions have shifted the focus towards defence capability, deterrence and preparedness.

At the same time, we know that military strength alone rarely creates long-term peace. Sustainable security also requires functioning institutions, diplomacy, conflict prevention and support for people affected by war and violence.

How can diplomacy, peacebuilding and military capability work together in an increasingly uncertain world? Do defence investments risk crowding out investments in peace? Or are they mutually dependent?

And what role can Sweden play in strengthening its own security while contributing to peace and stability internationally?

content.title: How can the state prevent failure and collapse in medicines policy?
content.description: New medicines can make a real difference, but the system for reimbursement and introduction is increasingly questioned. When treatments for serious common diseases are rejected, the question arises: is the state taking responsibility, and what does this cost patients?
content.extendedDescription: 1.5 million Swedes live with obesity. Hundreds of thousands of families are affected by Alzheimer's disease. These are two of the greatest public health challenges of our time, and we have treatments that can make a real difference. In Sweden, they become trapped in a system that sees them only as a cost, rather than the investment they actually are. TLV has rejected reimbursement for an obesity medicine despite acknowledging that it is unfortunate that no reimbursement solution could be found. And 35 leading researchers and doctors have described NT-rådet's rejection of an Alzheimer's medicine in a DN opinion article as a “shameful betrayal of patients”. The government has appointed an inquiry to reform a medicines system that the responsible minister says has reached “the end of the road”. But what should the state do, and do we have time to wait for an inquiry?

speakerTitles: State Secretary to Minister for Social Affairs Jakob Forssmed

content.title: Obesity care beyond medicines: creating modern, patient-centred treatment in practice
content.description: Swedish obesity care is at a crossroads. Practices differ between regions and knowledge-based governance lags behind, making care unequal and fragmented. When reimbursement issues determine priorities, patients risk falling through the gaps. How can care take the next step?
content.extendedDescription: Swedish obesity care is at a crossroads. Socialstyrelsen's first national evaluation of obesity care shows that hundreds of thousands of patients are not receiving care. Knowledge-based governance lags behind and practices differ between regions, making care unequal and fragmented. Meanwhile, more coordinated, scalable care models are emerging, with long-term support combining medical follow-up, behavioural change and digital tools. When reimbursement issues determine priorities, progress risks slowing and patients fall through the gaps. The seminar discusses how Swedish obesity care can take the next step: separating knowledge-based governance from reimbursement, creating clearer care pathways and strengthening equity in treatment and follow-up.
