content.title: What happens to the electronics tax after the election?
content.description: The electronics tax is added directly to the price when you buy electronics and household appliances. Swedish households pay around SEK 2.7 billion annually, going straight into the public treasury. The tax was supposed to provide environmental benefits but has not done so. Why does it remain?
content.extendedDescription:
A discussion of the electronics tax, sometimes called the chemicals tax: an additional tax on household appliances and consumer electronics found only in Sweden which, despite its ambition, has delivered no environmental benefit. It is added to the product price and based on product weight. The electronics tax can increase the price of a television, computer or household appliance by up to SEK 690. VAT is then charged on the tax. Consumers therefore pay not only the tax but also tax on the tax, making games consoles more expensive in Sweden than in other markets.

What do prospective MPs actually think of the tax, how could it be abolished, and what consequences has it had for Swedish businesses?

content.extendedDescription:
As global uncertainty increases, the links between energy systems, industrial competitiveness and national security are becoming more evident. Electrification plays a central role in enabling a more resilient, sustainable and independent Europe. content.title: Has Sweden's medicines system reached the end of the road?
content.description: What lies ahead for Sweden's medicines system and the changes the government has announced by appointing an inquiry? Will the state assume broader and stronger responsibility for medicines and vaccines?
content.extendedDescription:
The extensive geopolitical changes, increased competition and unpredictability of recent years have put pressure on individual countries' medicines systems. Swedish healthcare is of high quality, but the number of clinical trials is declining, and access primarily to new medicines, especially orphan drugs and oncology medicines, appears to be decreasing compared with other countries. Against this background, among other factors, the government's Minister for Health and Social Affairs has stated that the system needs to change and appointed an inquiry for this purpose. In this discussion, we will hear the government's arguments for changing the system and different stakeholders' views on the needs to be addressed.

KI Science Park Lunch Talks is a collaboration between KI Science Park (KI Innovation), Bayer and Waters. It is a recurring series of discussions held twice per semester at KI Campus Solna and, on this occasion, during Almedalsveckan.

content.title: Access to healthcare – why are more resources not enough to shorten waiting lists?
content.description: Swedish healthcare receives more resources than before, yet access has not improved at the expected pace. Waiting lists for specialist care have grown, more people wait longer than the care guarantee allows, and many patients find it difficult to contact healthcare services.
content.extendedDescription: Kunskapsverket's report How Is Healthcare Doing?, for which Sirona supported the analysis, shows that the regions' healthcare costs per resident increased by 18 per cent between 2010 and 2022, while the number of healthcare contacts per resident rose by only 2 per cent. During the seminar, we discuss what is actually preventing better access: a lack of resources, governance, administration, skills provision or how healthcare capacity is used? The aim is to move beyond the question of ‘more money’ and discuss which changes can actually give patients faster, closer and more coordinated care.

content.title: Capital for gender equality — future financing for sustainable development
content.description: How can new financial solutions mobilise capital for women's rights and economic equality?
content.extendedDescription:
Although gender equality is essential to sustainable development, only a small share of the world's capital goes towards women's rights and gender equality. At the same time, interest is growing in impact investing, sustainable financial markets and innovative financial solutions that can generate both social change and long-term economic development.

Gender bonds, gender-lens investing and fintech for financial inclusion are attracting increasing attention in Sweden and internationally. Banks, investors, development aid organisations, international organisations and civil society are exploring how capital markets can be used to strengthen women's economic empowerment and finance gender equality work on a larger scale.

The discussion brings together participants from the public sector, financial sector, international organisations and civil society to discuss how innovative financing models can contribute to gender equality and sustainable development — in Sweden and globally.

content.title: The integration policy of the future
content.description: The integration debate is increasingly marked by smears and oversimplification. Meanwhile, real problems relating to work, housing, language and discrimination persist. How do we create integration policy that actually works and gives people opportunities to establish themselves and contribute?
content.extendedDescription:
Sweden needs a new integration policy. In recent years, immigrants have increasingly been made scapegoats in public debate. This fuels polarisation and racism while shifting attention away from real integration problems.
Following a tour of Sweden from Skurup to Boden, Integrationsbyrån presents 31 reform proposals for better, more humane and effective integration policy. The proposals draw on conversations with people around the country, civil society experience and research into what actually strengthens integration.
The seminar addresses work, education, housing, discrimination and the role of civil society — but also what kind of society Sweden wants to be. How do we create a society in which more people can establish themselves, feel hopeful about the future and contribute their skills? And how do we move beyond an integration debate stuck in suspicion and symbolic politics?

content.title: Strengthen the law against genital mutilation
content.description: Female genital mutilation is a serious human rights violation. Despite the ban, a widely discussed court case found that mutilation of a girl's internal genital organs was not covered by the legislation. How should the law be revised to cover all forms of genital mutilation?
content.extendedDescription:
Female genital mutilation is a serious violation of girls' bodily integrity and human rights. Although it has been prohibited in Sweden since 1982, shortcomings remain in the law's wording and application.

In a widely discussed Swedish court case, a procedure on a girl's internal genital organs was found not to fall under the law and was instead handled as assault. This suggests current legislation does not cover all forms of mutilating procedures.

Why should legislation against genital mutilation be strengthened to cover all forms? How can prevention, detection and prosecution of genital mutilation affecting girls resident in Sweden be improved?

GAPF believes the legislation should be clarified to explicitly cover procedures on internal genital organs. Sweden should have zero tolerance for genital mutilation.

content.title: How can we prevent children being taken abroad against their will?
content.description: Every year after the summer holidays, some classroom desks remain empty. Most children taken abroad against their will in 2022 were already known to social services, but were taken out of the country before authorities acted. Schools and social services need to identify pupils at risk before it is too late.
content.extendedDescription:
Every year after the summer holidays, some classroom desks remain empty. GAPF attempted to help bring home 47 children taken abroad against their will in 2025.

GAPF has worked with five municipalities and Stockholms universitet to produce evidence to strengthen this work. Devin Rexvid presents findings from his review of judgments under the Care of Young Persons Act (LVU), showing important qualitative differences between children exposed to honour-based violence and other children. Sara Mohammad presents the results of a survey of school staff's experiences of honour-related cases.

The study and survey form the basis of a handbook on children taken abroad against their will, intended to help professionals make better risk and protection assessments. The project is financially supported by Postkodlotteriets stiftelse and Bertil Strömbergs stiftelse.

The handbook will be distributed at the seminar.

content.title: How do we ensure more reports of honour-related crime lead to prosecution?
content.description: The honour killings of Pela Atroshi in 1999 and Fadime Shahindal opened Sweden's eyes to honour-related abuse, and important legislative reforms followed. Yet very few reports lead to prosecution. Does the justice system have the knowledge and resources needed for honour-related cases?
content.extendedDescription:
During 2025, GAPF's support service had contact with over 360 people subjected to honour-related violence. Many faced serious threats. Few had police protection or other support. None were involved in ongoing investigations into honour-based oppression.

Meanwhile, Brottsförebyggande rådet's new report on honour-based oppression legislation lacks an important element: victims' perspectives. The justice system has a vital role in investigating and prosecuting honour-related crime. GAPF identifies major shortcomings in the report's conclusions and the justice system's handling of these cases.

• Why do so few reports lead to prosecution?

• Do police, prosecutors and courts have sufficient knowledge of honour-related crime?

The event is for everyone working in law enforcement – police officers, prosecutors, judges and politicians – as well as schools and social services, often the first to suspect honour-related crime.
content.subject: Justice/crime

content.title: Ban gender-segregated swimming sessions
content.description: Honour culture naturally supports gender-segregated swimming sessions: girls' and women's bodies must not be seen by any man other than a husband. Such sessions have been justified as a way to improve swimming skills among girls otherwise forbidden to swim. In practice, however, they reinforce discrimination.
content.extendedDescription:
A lecture on the consequences of gender-segregated swimming sessions and how gender segregation undermines equality, followed by a panel discussion.

Honour culture naturally supports gender-segregated swimming sessions: girls' and women's bodies must not be seen by any man other than a husband, while their brothers and husbands do as they please. Such sessions have been justified as a way to improve swimming skills among girls otherwise forbidden to swim at all. In practice, however, they reinforce discrimination.

Girls in honour cultures grow up ashamed of their bodies, and society's acceptance of this view of women's bodies confirms their families' honour norms. Some girls of compulsory school age are not allowed to attend swimming lessons but must swim at gender-segregated sessions to pass physical education.

GAPF strongly opposes gender-segregated swimming sessions. They conflict with democracy and gender equality and allow oppressive norms to grow stronger.
content.subject: Gender equality
speakerTitles: Researcher on Honour-Related Violence and Oppression

content.title: Why the delay in newborn screening? A system one step behind, and what politics can do
content.description: Delayed diagnosis of cystic fibrosis can cause unnecessary suffering and poorer health for children. This matters because Sweden lacks national newborn screening for the disease, although early detection enables prompt treatment and better quality of life.
content.extendedDescription: In March 2026, Socialstyrelsen was tasked with reviewing its model for national screening programmes. This is welcome, but to make a difference the review must address a fundamental shortcoming: decisions on newborn screening for new diseases take too long. Cystic fibrosis (CF) is a clear example. Sweden screens newborns for 24 serious inherited diseases, but not CF, although most European countries do and effective treatments are available from a very early age. For a progressive disease such as CF, every month's delay can affect health and quality of life. The issue is therefore not only medical possibilities, but also how quickly society's decision-making processes can adapt as knowledge and treatment develop.

content.title: Are Swedish companies equipped for tomorrow's skills needs?
content.description: The skills transition is already here, but many organisations still lack the ability to address today's capacity shortages and tomorrow's skills needs simultaneously. This goes beyond individual companies: how do we build a labour market capable of rapid adaptation and long-term skills development?
content.extendedDescription:
Drawing on fresh data from Wise in cooperation with Novus, the seminar takes a fact-based look at how Swedish organisations work to meet their skills needs today and what is required, at both company and system level, to meet future needs.

Together with our panel, we discuss:
• How short-term decisions affect organisations' ability to meet long-term skills needs.
• What trade-offs are needed between developing existing skills and recruiting new ones.
• How organisations can create structures that enable learning, mobility and continuous adaptation.

By combining data, research and perspectives from business, the social partners and politics, we develop a shared picture of the current situation and discuss the structural choices needed for Sweden to navigate the transition with both speed and staying power.

content.title: Heta stubben: Swedes are world leaders in sedentary behaviour – what will it take to reverse the trend?
content.description: Four in five children spend too much time sitting still, and the trend shows no sign of reversing. What is needed to mobilise efforts for more physical activity? What new approaches can reduce sitting and increase movement? Perhaps more exercise and physical activity without having to compete?
content.extendedDescription:
Last year’s Almedalen success, Heta stubben, is back. With the sea as a backdrop and the aroma of boiled coffee from the outdoor stove, Friluftsfrämjandet will hold conversations with party leaders and other decision-makers on various occasions about their vision for outdoor recreation. How can outdoor recreation and nature activities have as natural a place in politics as they do in our hearts? How can more people be encouraged to be physically active in nature? How can outdoor recreation help strengthen preparedness?

Four out of five children get too little physical activity, and half of adults have fitness levels so poor that they put their health at risk. Sedentary lifestyles and mental ill health cost society five per cent of GDP. This is deeply problematic for individuals, public health and Swedes’ resilience in crises. At the same time, we know that investment in physical activity is highly profitable.

The upkeep of our nature reserves and national parks is severely neglected, even though we know that spending time in attractive natural surroundings benefits our physical and mental health.

content.title: A journey through Sweden: diversity, inclusion and what actually works
content.description: Sweden faces both a growing skills shortage and widespread exclusion. Although many people want to and can work, they still encounter barriers to entering working life. Which measures work in practice to make better use of skills and strengthen integration?
content.extendedDescription:
Diversity and inclusion are high on the agenda in most organisations. Yet the gap between intention and reality is well known. What actually makes a difference, and what is mostly about looking good?

Aaron Kroon has travelled around Sweden, meeting leaders and employees across the country. His conversations with people on the ground have given him a picture of integration and inclusion that is rarely seen in public debate: nuanced, sometimes surprising and always rooted in reality.

The discussion concludes with questions from the audience.

content.title: When AI changes the rules – is human capability our most important competitive advantage?
content.description: AI is rapidly changing what creates value in an organisation. Processes and technical capacity are becoming easier to copy. What remains is judgement, prioritisation and the ability to make people, technology and business goals work together. How do we build organisations that strengthen the human dimension in the AI era?
content.extendedDescription:
Using fresh data from Wise in cooperation with Novus, the seminar takes a fact-based look at how Swedish organisations develop human capability and what is needed to make it a genuine business strategy in an AI-driven economy.

Together with our panel, we discuss:
• Which capabilities become most crucial as change, digitalisation and AI accelerate.
• How our view of capability influences team building, leadership development and organisational design.
• What is needed to move from intuitive assessment to a more systematic and accurate approach.

Combining data, research and perspectives from business, the social partners and politics, we develop a shared picture of what making human capability a business strategy actually means, and which choices determine whether organisations fully benefit from AI.

The seminar is held in cooperation with Sveriges HR-Förening and Fabege.

content.title: Young people's influence. Regional strength.
content.description: Young people from different parts of the country, backgrounds and age groups want to have a say. Yet there is a lack of ongoing forums where young people can influence all areas of regional responsibility. Can regional youth councils fill this gap and enable young people to exert influence?
content.extendedDescription:
Over the past three years, Sveriges ungdomsråd has worked on the Regional Youth Project, funded by Allmänna Arvsfonden, which aims to narrow the distance between young people, regional services and regional politics. Together with regions, we work to strengthen young people's participation, influence and organisation at regional level. We share challenges and lessons relating to involving a broad group of young people in decision-making through the regional youth council method.

Visit us and talk to young people from 7 different regions who have engaged in regional issues, helped establish regional youth councils and played an active part in the Regional Youth Project. Together, we look ahead: what is needed to continue strengthening young people's voices in the regions? You can also test your own knowledge of regions, share your views or perhaps take part in a mini-interview.

Young people's influence is a regional strength that we all have a responsibility to make use of.

content.title: Knowledge or money – what determines Swedish obesity care?
content.description: On 1 June, Sweden received new national clinical guidance on obesity – but is the treatment that healthcare professionals know works reaching patients? Effective medicines are not subsidised and are not recommended, and healthcare providers are urged to wait until the disease becomes severe. Is care guided by knowledge – or by money?
content.extendedDescription:
This is an open roundtable discussion – everyone present is welcome to listen and follow the conversation around the table. We discuss what really determines Swedish obesity care in practice: knowledge and medical need, or subsidies.
The new clinical guidance raises several questions. Why, in practice, is an older medicine recommended over more effective ones? And why should care providers wait until a patient has severe obesity with complications, instead of treating the condition earlier and preventing them?
Meanwhile, Socialstyrelsen has evaluated obesity care and identified major shortcomings: few regions have an action plan, follow-up is weak, and the newer, more effective medicines are not covered by the high-cost protection scheme. Patients currently pay virtually the entire cost of medication, while regional costs have barely increased – resulting in increasingly unequal care.
What is needed to ensure that the treatment healthcare professionals know works best actually reaches patients – and who must act?

content.title: What is happening to Sweden's startup and innovation policy?
content.description: There is broad political agreement that innovation matters – but what does that mean in practice? What do parties promise on Vinnova, innovation vouchers, employee stock options and startup visas?
content.extendedDescription:
Innovation is among the most important drivers of Swedish prosperity and job creation, yet innovation policy risks being sidelined during the election campaign.

Sweden's innovation ecosystem is strong, but conditions are deteriorating. International competition for talent and capital is intensifying. Regulatory complexity and tax conditions make starting and scaling companies harder, and national co-financing to secure EU funding is not fully used.

Ahead of the 2026 election, SISP asked all parliamentary parties the same seven questions. Results in Innovationsvalbarometern 2026 reveal clear differences and gaps deserving debate.
The event is a roundtable with eight participants; audience members are welcome to follow the discussion.
content.subject: Innovation

content.title: How free and independent are public service broadcasters and other tax-funded media?
content.description: Tax-funded media are often described as ‘free and independent’, but is that true if they also depend on tax funding? How have new challengers in the media market affected traditional media?
content.extendedDescription:
As tax-funded media face competition from new technology platforms and publishers, traditional media platforms are losing their privilege to define the issues and being challenged by an entirely new media community. What are the consequences when the tax-funded remit of Sweden's largest media organisation, public service broadcasting, is increasingly questioned and criticised for a lack of factual accuracy and impartiality?

Why have the Tidö parties avoided addressing the problems public service broadcasters are increasingly found to have? What allows SVT and SR to escape consequences for internal activism, such as the appeal concerning Swedish media reporting on Gaza, and double standards for participation in public service productions?

Opinion-maker Josefin Utas discusses these questions with public commentator Nick Alinia. Lena Malmberg (MED) moderates the discussion.
content.subject: Democracy

content.title: How do we secure the energy of the future?
content.description: What does a green transition mean? Do we save the climate by reducing electricity consumption, or by increasing it? Does building nuclear power plants have to take a long time? Are wind turbines a solution or an environmental hazard?
content.extendedDescription: The panel takes the form of an open discussion led by a moderator. The audience will also have the opportunity to ask questions and comment. The aim is to move beyond party politics and use common sense and scientific truths in physics and economics to find a way forward for Sweden. Why do we need electricity? What happens without growth? How does Denmark manage without nuclear power plants? How long does a wind turbine last? Is a shared EU electricity market a good or a bad thing? Does it make sense for the state to invest in "green" projects? If not, why should the state subsidise nuclear power, or wind power? The aim of the discussion is to encourage participants to deepen their understanding of and interest in energy issues.
content.subject: Energy
speakerTitles: Lawyer, Deputy Chair of MED Sthlm stad

content.title: How can shipping become a first-choice career?
content.description: How can Sweden secure the skills needed in shipping as demand for staff increases? The challenge spans the entire chain, from education and recruitment to opportunities to develop, remain in the sector and build a lifelong maritime career.
content.extendedDescription:
Shipping is a key industry for Sweden's trade, preparedness and climate transition. At the same time, it faces significant challenges in attracting, training and retaining skilled staff. Meeting future needs requires collaboration between business, education providers and political decision-makers.

The seminar discusses how more people can be inspired to choose a maritime career, how the education system can meet industry needs and what measures are needed to create sustainable long-term career paths.

Hear shipping companies and decision-makers share experiences, identify barriers and present solutions to strengthen skills provision and competitiveness in Swedish shipping. Together, we discuss how the maritime industry of the future can secure the right skills at the right time.
content.subject: Infrastructure/transport
speakerTitles: Head of the Ships and Seaworthiness Unit

content.title: Data centres are crucial to Sweden's competitiveness
content.description: Data centres underpin AI, digitalisation and future growth. How do we ensure Sweden remains competitive in the global race for investment, innovation and digital infrastructure?

Data centres are increasingly highlighted as a key factor in Sweden's competitiveness, with major potential for investment, employment and innovation. content.title: Does Sweden have the energy to become a leading AI nation – or will electricity become the next bottleneck?
content.description:
AI could become Sweden's next major competitive advantage, but it comes at a price: energy.
As AI moves from experimentation to business-critical infrastructure, demands for electricity, data centres and capacity are growing at an unprecedented pace. Meanwhile, all of society must electrify, from industry to transport.
content.extendedDescription:
AI is often treated as a software issue today. In practice, however, it is a physical reality, powered by energy, computing capacity and infrastructure. In this panel, we ask the crucial question and discuss:

How AI actually affects Sweden's energy needs
Whether data centres should be prioritised in the energy system
Whether data centres can supply energy and how to think sustainably and innovatively when developing for AI
How to balance AI growth with society's electrification
What is needed for Sweden to attract and retain AI investment

Join a focused discussion where AI is about not only technology but power, priorities and future competitiveness.
content.subject: Energy

content.title: Girls and women with lipoedema receive neither a correct diagnosis nor care
content.description: 5–10 per cent of women live with the painful disease lipoedema. Research shows that they wait decades for a correct diagnosis and have to pay for their own care. Swedish healthcare is failing girls and women with lipoedema. Would you like to help change this?
content.extendedDescription:
A neglected common disease – a gender equality issue
According to researchers, one in ten women has lipoedema, a disease that is very painful and disabling for many women. Research shows that most experience a severely reduced quality of life. Despite this, healthcare services do not take this hereditary disease seriously.
There is no cure, but various treatments can relieve symptoms; however, women must pay for these themselves.
In its report, the SÖSR methods council argues that withholding multidisciplinary care, including publicly provided liposuction, from patients with lipoedema is incompatible with the spirit of the Health and Medical Services Act.
Would you like to learn more about symptoms and treatment, and what it is like to live with lipoedema?
Do you work in healthcare and want to learn how to diagnose lipoedema?
As a person with responsibility, a decision-maker or a politician, would you like to learn more about what you can do to change this situation?
What will you and your party do about the situation over the next four years?
content.subject: Health and social care

content.description: Sweden needs more companies that grow, create jobs, attract capital and strengthen our competitiveness. At the same time, there is substantial untapped potential. content.title: Can Sweden and the US build nuclear faster for Europe?
content.description: Europe needs more dispatchable clean energy. Advanced nuclear reactors could be part of the answer, but getting there requires capital, regulation and cross-border collaboration. What structures do we need to actually bring new nuclear to market in time?
content.extendedDescription:
Blykalla and Oklo use different technologies – liquid lead and sodium respectively – but share the same conviction: that the transatlantic relationship is the fastest route to commercial nuclear power. They are part-competitors, part-partners, and have chosen to invest in each other.

In this fireside chat, Blykalla CEO Jacob Stedman and Oklo CEO Jacob DeWitte get candid about what it actually takes to build a new kind of nuclear company: the capital, the regulation, the timelines – and why co-opetition turned out to be the smartest move. What does it mean for Sweden, for US-European energy ties, and for the pace of the energy transition?

content.title: The blue investment grant – how could it support clean water throughout Sweden?
content.description: 240,000 properties still lack approved wastewater treatment. Phosphorus leaks into lakes and the Baltic Sea while the pace of action stagnates. The blue investment grant could reverse this trend, but how should support be designed to encourage more property owners to act?
content.extendedDescription:
Representatives of MRV and Villaägarnas riksförbund present, together with the audience, the initiative Det blå investeringsbidraget: a concrete proposal for making approved wastewater treatment financially accessible to property owners nationwide.

Sweden has 419,000 kilometres of shoreline and bears full responsibility for its own lakes and watercourses. Yet almost a quarter of a million properties lack approved treatment.

Technology is not the problem. Financial incentives are missing. For individual property owners, the investment feels unaffordable without support. Meanwhile, municipal water and wastewater finances face investment needs of 31 billion kronor annually: every property treating its own wastewater is one the municipality need not connect by pipeline.

The proposed blue investment grant would be included in the green technology tax deduction framework and could provide the boost needed to finally increase the pace of action.

Coffee, sandwiches and drinks will be served.

content.title: How can the Nordic region strengthen Europe's competitiveness?
content.description: As Europe falls behind in global competition, the Nordic region remains strong in industry, technology and capital. How can a more integrated Nordic region bring together companies, investors and decision-makers to create the next generation of industrial initiatives and become an engine of European growth?
content.extendedDescription:
Geopolitical tensions, technological transition and tougher global competition are changing conditions for European business. Meanwhile, the Nordic region has unique strengths: world-leading companies, strong capital markets, considerable innovative capacity and close interaction between business, research and society.
Against this backdrop, Nordic Compass has been established as a Nordic alliance of leading companies, investors and foundations aiming to strengthen the region's competitiveness.
Leading representatives of business, finance and politics discuss how the Nordic region can play a more active role in strengthening Europe's competitiveness. What investments, reforms and partnerships are needed? How can Nordic cooperation accelerate innovation, attract capital and build the industries of the future? And what role can Nordic Compass play in shaping the next chapter of Nordic growth, competitiveness and industrial development?

content.title: Always prepared — together for a better world
content.description: In a time of crises and uncertainty, we need to strengthen society's resilience and safeguard children's and young people's safety, participation and confidence in the future. How can meaningful leisure activities contribute to stronger preparedness, trust and democracy?
content.extendedDescription:
Scouts are always prepared. Prepared for adventures in nature, for challenging situations and for one another. We believe in — and act for — a democratic and peaceful world in which young people have a say. That is building real resilience.

Resilience is not only about handling a crisis. It also involves the broader preparedness built when people help one another, take responsibility, cooperate and trust their own and others' abilities. In Scouterna, children and young people gain both practical skills and the courage to use them — for one another and for society. Resilience also means strengthening what is worth defending: democracy, peace and trust.

Welcome to Scouterna's camp in the middle of Almedalen! Try scouting activities and learn more about how children and young people in Scouterna develop skills for life and the power to make the world better for more people. We also offer popcorn made on a camping stove!

content.title: How can we strengthen and support municipalities' efforts against welfare crime in public procurement?
content.description: What challenges do municipalities and other public purchasing organisations face when criminal actors try to exploit public contracts and welfare systems? What measures and practical support can strengthen prevention, follow-up and collaboration?
content.extendedDescription:
Welfare crime and infiltration of public procurement by unscrupulous or criminal actors risk undermining trust in public purchasing. When taxpayers' money goes to companies whose business models involve fraud, labour-related crime or organised crime, competition is distorted, welfare service quality may deteriorate and society's resilience weakens.

How can municipalities and other public purchasing organisations use procurement to counter these risks?

A panel representing municipalities, authorities and other relevant stakeholders discusses practical experience, operational support and good examples of how procurement can help prevent and detect welfare crime. content.title: When AI democratises branding — who is in control?
content.description: Generative AI turns more people into content creators — and brand builders. The opportunities are substantial, but so is the growing risk that a brand will be disseminated and interpreted without a coherent whole. What holds a brand together when more employees, partners and resellers create content?
content.extendedDescription:
Generative AI turns more people within a company into content producers and, consequently, brand builders. The opportunities are enormous, but for large organisations this also brings a new risk: that the brand is disseminated, interpreted and used without anyone truly holding the whole together. This raises the question of what holds a brand together when creation increasingly spreads to employees, partners, resellers and others.

The panel explores the tension between speed and coherence. We highlight examples of what happens when AI relies on outdated guidelines, incorrect input or a weak understanding of the brand. Where is the boundary between healthy decentralisation and dilution of what we want to achieve with the brand? Is ‘control’ even the right ambition, or is it about embedding the brand so deeply that it can withstand being created by many?
content.subject: Digitalisation

content.title: Higher returns and impact through blended finance?

content.title: 19,700 children a year – who catches them when school adjustments disappear?
content.description: Every year, almost 20,000 pupils leave compulsory school without eligibility for upper secondary education. The biggest school reform in 30 years is now being implemented. Does it meet the needs of children who are struggling and failing at school, or abandon them?
content.extendedDescription:
One in six pupils leaves compulsory school without eligibility for upper secondary education, a figure unchanged for decades. Behind it are children with growing mental ill health, increasing absence and paths often leading to exclusion. Many have neurodevelopmental conditions or other support needs that today's schools do not meet.
From 2028, new curricula will follow children's cognitive development. At the same time, additional adjustments and the guarantee of early support are being abolished. Signs often appear in the early primary years. The question is what failing to identify them in time costs.
Does the reform meet the needs of children who are struggling and failing at school, or abandon them?
A discussion about mental ill health, exclusion and what is needed in practice.

content.title: From AI to Impact: Securing Competitive and Equitable Growth
content.description: Sweden faces slowing productivity, shortage of talent, and rising global competition. How can AI drive real growth—by building trust, ensuring security, scaling adoption, and embedding AI across sectors to boost productivity and inclusive value creation?
content.extendedDescription:
Sweden faces a structural growth challenge marked by slowing productivity, demographic pressure, and intensifying global competition. While AI is often framed as a risk or compliance issue, its core economic potential—boosting productivity and value creation—remains underexplored. This panel starts from a clear premise: AI delivers national impact only when trust, security, and scale are in place.
 
Building on Sweden’s national AI strategy, the discussion focuses on moving from vision to execution—embedding AI in core processes, investing in shared capabilities like data, platforms, and skills, and aligning innovation with regulation without slowing progress. Rather than replacing jobs, AI can augment human capability, speed decision-making, and scale expertise across sectors.
 
Drawing on global examples, the panel explores how to unlock equitable growth by ensuring AI benefits reach SMEs, public services, and all regions.

content.title: With AI we can produce more than ever – but are we creating more value?
content.description: AI enables us to produce more than ever – but is real value increasing at the same pace? When output grows faster than judgement, quality, trust and confidence are at stake. What role does communication play, and what leadership is needed for AI to create business value rather than just more content?
content.extendedDescription:
More and more organisations are embedding AI in processes and daily work. But its effects become visible first in marketing and communications. Here, AI strategy is tested in real time and choices are exposed: what is automated, what requires human judgement and what actually creates value?

Despite high ambitions, many still see limited business impact. Have we become better at producing, but not at deciding what is good? And what happens to brands when everything can be generated but fewer people take responsibility for quality, relevance and trust? The discussion is not about AI as technology, but about what AI reveals about how we lead, prioritise and build our organisations. The focus shifts from what AI can do to what organisations can actually use, understand and evaluate.

A moderated panel discussion for marketing and communications directors, brand managers and leaders navigating the shift between technology, business and customer relationships.

content.title: Equitable menopause care: why do not all women receive the treatment they need?
content.description: Access to menopause care and treatment in Sweden is currently unequal. Differences in access to gynaecologists, primary care knowledge and medicines mean many women do not receive the care they need, with consequences for both health and working life.
content.extendedDescription:
Although menopause affects a large part of the population, care is marked by significant inequalities. Access to specialist expertise varies between regions, and primary care knowledge is uneven, meaning many women do not receive the right diagnosis or treatment in time. The consequences are extensive. Women risk poorer quality of life, increased sickness absence and reduced work capacity. Particularly vulnerable groups, such as women with neurodevelopmental disabilities, are more likely to experience severe symptoms and inadequate support. Meanwhile, recurring shortages of important medicines further impede equitable treatment.

content.title: Uniform, Pride, trust – hate crime against LGBTQI people, safety and confidence in the police
content.description: Many LGBTQI people have less trust in the police and justice system than the population as a whole. Meanwhile, negative attitudes towards LGBTQI people are increasing, and hatred is taking new forms, both online and in everyday life. What is needed to strengthen safety and confidence in the police?
content.extendedDescription:
Trust in the police and justice system is an important part of a safe and democratic society. Yet RFSL's latest safety report shows that many LGBTQI people still feel less safe than the population as a whole and have lower confidence in the police and justice system. Several government agency reports also show increased negative attitudes towards LGBTQI people, growing anti-LGBTQI hostility in digital environments and continued exposure to hate crime.

The debate over police officers' ability to wear uniforms in Pride parades has brought questions of visibility, representation and trust to the fore. But what is needed for more people to feel safe in everyday life? How can hate crimes be prevented and investigated more effectively? What role do the police have in prevention, and how do we ensure that people subjected to hate crime receive equal treatment and support wherever they live in the country?

The seminar takes the form of a discussion between representatives of RFSL and Polisförbundet.
content.subject: Justice/crime

content.title: What LGBTQI policy can we expect after the 2026 election?
content.description: Many LGBTQI people feel increasingly unsafe while rights are being challenged in Sweden and internationally. Which LGBTQI reforms do the parties want to prioritise after the 2026 election?
content.extendedDescription:
RFSL's safety report shows that many LGBTQI people feel increasingly unsafe, have less confidence in the future and trust society's institutions less than the population as a whole. At the same time, negative attitudes towards LGBTQI people are increasing among young people, and LGBTQI rights are being restricted in many countries.

What reforms are needed to respond? How do the parties want to strengthen safety for LGBTQI people in daily life, online, at school and in encounters with the justice system? What responsibility does Sweden have for people fleeing persecution because of sexual orientation or gender identity? And which LGBTQI policy reforms will the parties prioritise during the next parliamentary term?

This discussion brings together representatives of parliamentary parties to give concrete answers about their priorities ahead of the 2026 election and the coming parliamentary term.

content.title: Producer responsibility for textiles: seamless or patchwork?
content.description: The EU is introducing extended producer responsibility for textiles, and Sweden must develop a system by 2028. The aim is to drive circularity through better collection, reuse and recycling. Yet uncertainty remains about how the system should be designed in practice and what impact it will actually have.
content.extendedDescription:
As EU regulations are implemented in Sweden, a national system for textile producer responsibility must be designed. This involves the division of responsibilities, funding and how collection and sorting will work in practice. Experience from other markets and existing systems is essential to avoiding inefficient solutions and unnecessary costs.

At the same time, companies are developing their work on circular design, reuse and recycling. How this interacts with the new regulations will determine whether circularity can be scaled up.

The discussion brings together politics and business to consider how producer responsibility can be designed to deliver real results and which priorities are needed going forward.

content.title: Scaling from Sweden – a compromise or a competitive advantage?
content.description: How can Sweden strengthen its ability to turn innovation into international growth, jobs and competitiveness? This matters because future prosperity depends heavily on whether new technology companies can grow from Sweden.
content.extendedDescription:
Sweden is strong at creating tech companies, and Swedish companies rank among the world's best at scaling. Talent and capital are important prerequisites, but customers are equally crucial. What role do established companies and public bodies play as the next generation of Swedish tech companies grows globally?

The discussion starts with Sweden as a base for scaling: is it a compromise, or can it become a clearer competitive advantage? For more companies to take the next step, talent and capital are needed, alongside partnerships extending beyond pilot projects and innovation programmes, giving smaller innovative companies access to early customers, strategic partners and real business.

The panel discusses building an ecosystem that optimises for upside, speed and future growth rather than reducing downside and preserving the status quo.
content.subject: Business

content.title: Should we shut down district heating, or does it have a future?
content.description: In recent years, many municipalities and their public housing companies have seen sharply rising district heating costs for public-service premises and homes.
content.extendedDescription:
Four municipalities in inland Västerbotten have joined a project to highlight rising district heating costs. None operates its own district heating; external operators own and run the systems. The municipalities now face a difficult situation as homeowners switch to other energy sources and municipalities themselves choose alternatives for new public-service properties. What happens when a town's district heating network is no longer considered profitable enough and the external operator withdraws? Small municipalities with declining populations lack investment funds to convert, and doing so would also destroy capital when a fully functioning district heating network already exists.

The seminar examines the current situation for district heating and discusses its possible future.

content.title: Honour-related violence – how did the issue emerge, and where are Sweden and the Nordic countries today?
content.description: Honour-related violence has been discussed as a political issue in Sweden for 30 years. How did debate begin? Which voices and victims came into focus? How have Nordic countries addressed it, and how do we balance recognition against invisibility?
content.extendedDescription:
Several widely reported, brutal murders of young women and a young man in the early 2000s put honour-related violence on Sweden's agenda. Society has since debated and acted against it. Action plans and legislation exist. But how did discussion and work against this violence begin here? How has policy developed in the Nordic countries? Do we know what makes an approach successful? How do we balance recognition against stigmatisation? Is Sweden extreme in its approach?

content.title: Major investment in a national test centre for digital solutions aims to future-proof Swedish industry
content.description: An investment of 300 million is now being made in a national test centre for digital solutions – to give Swedish companies a significant technological lead and shorten the path from innovation to a finished solution. content.extendedDescription: The government's digitalisation and AI strategies highlight the need to test and apply digital solutions and AI services – innovation environments where business and public sector organisations can collaborate. This discussion explores its background and purpose, and how the test centre will strengthen Sweden's capacity for innovation and competitiveness by giving companies a technological lead and shortening the path from innovation to a finished solution. The project is funded through the innovation and collaboration programme Avancerad Digitalisering, with support from Vinnova.

content.title: A holistic health ecosystem through digital twins – a digital copy of yourself
content.description: What if you had a digital twin of yourself that could help you understand how to optimise exercise, diet and treatment? What if all societal actors used this twin and worked together to move society as a whole in a healthier direction?
content.extendedDescription:
25 years of research at Linköpings universitet have produced a new, globally unique technology: a digital twin of the human body. It looks like you on the outside and can simulate and show what happens inside your body when you do different things, such as exercising, eating or taking medicine. If you become ill, you can ask your twin what has happened and what you can do. You can connect with other people and life stories similar to yours and see what they did to improve. These stories also come with explanatory models of why they improved.
This globally unique technology underpins a new excellence cluster, M4-HEALTH, a new model for health. M4-HEALTH comprises researchers from 14 Swedish universities and higher education institutions, is supported by 100+ companies and involves public agencies, voluntary organisations and others. You will hear about this technology and how it can affect research, the food industry, healthcare providers, occupational health, elderly care and more.

content.title: A digital twin of yourself: the foundation for a new health ecosystem
content.description: What would it be like to have access to all accumulated knowledge about the human body in a way that is relevant to you and your health right now? This is being developed through a so-called digital twin. How can it replace animal experiments and make society as a whole healthier?
content.extendedDescription:
Researchers at Linköpings universitet have developed a new, globally unique technology: a digital twin of the human body. It can compile all conceivable knowledge both about you specifically and about human health in general. Such knowledge can come from clinical trials, cell experiments, activity trackers, online forums and more. This twin can be used to replace animal experiments. It can also be used by various societal actors, such as the food industry, schools, sports clubs, healthcare, elderly care and occupational health services.
These new possibilities underpin a new excellence cluster, M4-HEALTH, comprising researchers from 14 universities and higher education institutions and supported by 100+ companies, public agencies, associations and others. At this event, you will hear from some of these actors and learn more about how to obtain your own twin, and how it can help move both your life and society as a whole in a healthier direction.

content.title: Democracy in the shadow of change – 50 decisions that have dismantled Swedish development aid
content.description: Swedish development aid is currently undergoing extensive changes. Decisions that have been implemented have undermined Sweden's international credibility and replaced democratic participation with top-down decisions ungrounded in research or the experience of organisations on the ground. What does this mean for the world's poorest people?
content.extendedDescription:
Swedish development aid is currently undergoing extensive changes. Decisions and methods have been implemented that have undermined Sweden's international credibility and replaced democratic participation with top-down decisions ungrounded in research or reality. In a short time, numerous decisions have affected priorities, working methods and relationships with civil society and the countries where Sweden operates. This development means greater political micromanagement and less room for long-term work, knowledge and local involvement. What will happen as efforts to prevent humanitarian disasters, epidemics and conflicts diminish, while China and Russia expand their presence to advance their geopolitical interests?

In this seminar, we present a review of 50 specific decisions and changes in Swedish development aid policy and discuss what is at stake for aid effectiveness, Sweden's international role and trust in policy.

content.title: Humans as masters of creation or relatives among other beings – different perspectives and consequences?
content.description: How do we experience our relationship with the rest of the planet? Are humans in charge, or are we all equally important and interconnected? What does it mean that our experiences differ? How does Svenska kyrkan view this from biblical and human perspectives? What do the performing arts think, and what do you think?
content.extendedDescription:
A warm welcome to an open public conversation with guests from Visby Stift and the performing arts collective Tellus°. The gathering begins with a special version of Tellus°#3: Sympoiesis, a physical performance that premiered in February at Naturhistoriska Museet in Gothenburg. The performance then transitions into the conversation, both taking place inside Visby Domkyrka.
Tellus°#3: Sympoiesis is a physical, multidisciplinary artwork in which voice, movement, music and video portray humanity's attempt to reconnect with the living world it has never really left. We journey out of the Anthropocene – a popular way of viewing our human-dominated and sometimes ruthless era – and glimpse the Chthulucene, a very different and at least equally true account of our world. Shaped by ancient mechanisms and collaborations between life and matter, constantly evolving symbioses and relationships between life, time and rhythm. Natural laws and phenomena that seem undeterred by restrictive norms, structures and behaviours.

content.title: Profitability is determined before the first ground is broken
content.description: The decisions with the greatest impact on a property's profitability and long-term value are often made before construction begins. Yet many projects focus on construction costs, while fewer focus on decisions affecting the property's operation, flexibility and development potential.
content.extendedDescription:
Building services and energy affect a property throughout its lifetime. They influence how the building is used, managed, adapted and developed.

At Hamnplan 222, we are displaying EkoNod's demonstration module. It offers a practical insight into how building services and energy can be viewed as a system, and how that perspective can influence a project's development.

Visit the module and discuss how earlier decisions can contribute to more profitable properties, lower project risk, greater flexibility over time and higher long-term property value.
